us-policy-positions:labor-workforce.loca.source: State code sites (IA, KS, MO, NC, OH, WI, UT, TX, ID, OR, FL, SC, MI, LA, AZ, WA, CO, AR), Eleventh Circuit en banc opinion (12/13/2019), NELP preemption brief (July 2017) and NYC agenda (Dec. 2025), NLC 'City Rights in an Era of Preemption' (2017/2018), UC Berkeley Labor Center local ordinance inventory (07/23/2026), all fetched September 2026.
us-policy-positions:labor-workforce.loca.note: Places first left out were read on 9/29/2026; any still unread take the most common answer among similar places, marked ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE.

US-AK.note: Home-rule boroughs and cities may exercise all legislative powers not prohibited by law or charter, and the list of home-rule limits in AS 29.10.200 (checked at https://www.akleg.gov/basis/statutes.asp?media=print&secStart=29.10.200&secEnd=29.10.200) says nothing about wages; no Alaska city has yet adopted one.

US-AL.note: Signed February 25, 2016, voiding Birmingham's $10.10 ordinance; the Eleventh Circuit (en banc, 2019) dismissed the challenge for lack of standing.

US-AR.note: Act 643 of 2017 (approved 03/24/2017, no emergency clause) bars counties, cities and towns from requiring a minimum or living wage above state or federal law.

US-AS.note: American Samoa sets its minimum wage by territorial statute and the federal schedule, and no village or county has wage-setting power under it.

US-AZ.note: Counties, cities and towns may set higher minimum wages by ordinance; Flagstaff and Tucson have done so.

US-CA.note: No state preemption; about 40 cities and counties, including Los Angeles, San Francisco and San Diego, have their own higher minimum wages.

US-CO.note: H.B. 19-1210 repealed the prior ban on local minimum wages; Denver, Edgewater and Boulder County have since adopted them.

US-CT.note: Connecticut sets one statewide minimum wage under chapter 558 and neither authorizes nor bars a local minimum wage, and no Connecticut town or city has adopted one.

US-DC.note: D.C. has no state above it; the D.C. Council sets a local minimum wage above the federal rate (ordinance dates from 1992).

US-DE.note: Delaware sets one statewide minimum wage under 19 Del. C. chapter 9 and neither authorizes nor bars a local minimum wage, and no Delaware city or county has adopted one.

US-FL.note: The statute (ch. 2003-87) bars local minimum wages, though Fla. Const. art. X, § 24(f) says the amendment does not limit any public body from requiring higher wages; ch. 2024-80 tightens the ban (adds 'maintain' and contractor wage rules) effective 09/30/2026.

US-GA.note: Georgia preempts every local wage or employment benefit mandate and bars counties and cities from adopting, keeping or enforcing one (enacted by Ga. L. 2004, p. 377).

US-GU.cite: 22 Guam Code Ann. ch. 3, art. 1 (§ 3101 et seq.)
US-GU.note: Guam sets one territorywide minimum wage in its Minimum Wage and Hour Act and gives its villages no wage-setting power, though nothing in it expressly bars one.

US-HI.note: Hawaii sets one statewide minimum wage under chapter 387 and neither authorizes nor bars a county minimum wage, and no Hawaii county has adopted one.

US-IA.note: Ordinances adopted before 03/30/2017 were voided, including the Johnson, Linn, Polk, Lee and Wapello County wages.

US-ID.note: Section history lists amendments in 2007 and 2016 (ch. 145); the exact date subsection (4) took effect was not confirmed.

US-IL.note: Home-rule units may set higher wages; Chicago and Cook County have (many Cook County municipalities have opted out of the county rate).

US-IN.note: A unit of local government may not establish, mandate or require a minimum wage above the state or federal rate (added by P.L. 211-2011).

US-KS.note: Bars cities and counties from requiring wages above the minimum wage unless state or federal law requires them; enacted 2013 per NELP.

US-KY.cite: KRS 337.275 (as construed in Ky. Restaurant Ass'n v. Louisville/Jefferson County Metro Gov't, Ky. 2016)
US-KY.note: No express statute; the Kentucky Supreme Court held in 2016 that the state wage law leaves no room for local minimums, voiding the Louisville and Lexington ordinances.

US-MA.note: Massachusetts sets one statewide minimum wage under chapter 151 and neither authorizes nor bars a local minimum wage, and no Massachusetts city or town has adopted one.

US-MD.note: Montgomery and Howard Counties have local minimum wages above the state rate.

US-ME.note: No state preemption found; Portland and Rockland have local minimum wages above the state rate.

US-MI.note: Local Government Labor Regulatory Limitation Act, 2015 PA 105, immediate effect.

US-MN.note: Minneapolis and St. Paul have local minimum wages above the state rate.

US-MO.note: H.B. 1194 & 1193 (2017) nullified the St. Louis ordinance after the state supreme court struck the older 1998 ban (RSMo 67.1571) on single-subject grounds.

US-MP.note: The Northern Mariana Islands set one territorywide minimum wage in 4 CMC section 9221 and give municipalities no wage-setting power, though nothing in it expressly bars one.

US-MS.note: Cited by NELP (July 2017) among states that bar local minimum wages; the state code text itself was not reachable.

US-MT.note: Self-government units are denied any power to require a private employer to pay a wage or benefit not required by state or federal law (subsection (2) also bars acting on Title 39, the labor title); the section history lists several 2021 amendments, and which one added (23) was not confirmed.

US-NC.note: Current subsection (d), added by S.L. 2023-134, s. 5.9(a), preempts local rules on private-employer pay; the earlier subsection (c) from the 2016 law was repealed by S.L. 2017-4.

US-ND.note: Weak: North Dakota applies Dillon's Rule (Wikipedia table) and home-rule cities get only the powers enumerated in § 40-05.1-06, which list no wage power; the general-welfare ordinance power in subsection 10 has not been tested on wages.

US-NE.note: Nebraska has no statute barring local minimum wages, and Omaha has its own local minimum wage ordinance (Lincoln adopted one in 2026, effective after 1/1/2026).

US-NH.note: Weak: New Hampshire follows Dillon's Rule with no home rule (Wikipedia table), and the town bylaw powers in RSA 31:39 (https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/III/31/31-39.htm) list no wage power.

US-NJ.note: New Jersey sets one statewide minimum wage under its Wage and Hour Law and neither authorizes nor bars a local minimum wage, and no New Jersey municipality has adopted one.

US-NM.note: Santa Fe city and county, Las Cruces and Albuquerque have local minimum wages.

US-NV.note: Weak: Nevada keeps Dillon's Rule except for city 'matters of local concern', a term that excludes matters needing statewide uniformity and business activities subject to substantial state regulation, and no statute grants wage-setting power.

US-NY.cite: N.Y. Labor Law § 652 (as construed in Wholesale Laundry Bd. of Trade v. City of New York, 1962)
US-NY.note: No express statute; a 1962 court ruling holds cities cannot set their own minimum wage, and advocates argue it could be reconsidered; the higher NYC/Long Island/Westchester rates are set by state law.

US-OK.note: Cited by NELP (July 2017) among states that bar local minimum wages; the statute text was not reachable (oscn.net bot challenge).

US-OR.note: Enacted 2001 (ch. 967); local governments may set wages only for their own employees, contracts and subsidies; the Portland-metro, standard and nonurban tiers are set by state law (ORS 653.025).

US-PA.note: Philadelphia states it is preempted by Act 112 from passing any minimum wage law.

US-PR.cite: P.R. Laws Ann. tit. 29, § 245 et seq. (Ley 180-1998; Ley 47-2021)
US-PR.note: Puerto Rico sets one territorywide minimum wage by law (Law 180-1998, as amended by Law 47-2021) and gives municipalities no wage-setting power, though nothing in it expressly bars one.

US-RI.note: Cited by NELP (July 2017) among states that bar local minimum wages; the state statute site was not reachable from this environment.

US-SC.note: Enacted by 2002 Act No. 243; bars local minimum wages above the federal rate.

US-SD.note: Only home-rule charter units qualify: their ordinances may set standards higher than state law unless a state law provides otherwise, though SDCL 6-12-6(1) withholds power over private civil relationships and no local wage has been tested.

US-TN.note: Cited by NELP (July 2017) among states that bar local minimum wages; the state code text was not reachable.

US-TX.note: The state minimum wage supersedes local wage ordinances for private employment, except public contracts.

US-UT.note: Cities, towns and counties may not require a minimum wage above the federal minimum; last amended 2005.

US-VA.cite: Va. Code § 15.2-1102 (charter powers, read under Dillon's Rule)
US-VA.note: Weak: Virginia follows Dillon's Rule with no home rule (Wikipedia table); the general-welfare charter powers in Va. Code § 15.2-1102 (https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title15.2/chapter11/section15.2-1102/) grant no wage power in terms, and no Virginia locality has one.

US-VI.note: The Virgin Islands sets its minimum wage through a territorial wage board and has no local governments that could set their own.

US-VT.note: Weak: Vermont follows Dillon's Rule with no home rule (Wikipedia table), and the enumerated municipal powers in 24 V.S.A. § 2291 include no power to set wages.

US-WA.note: State law is a floor that leaves more favorable local wage ordinances in force; Seattle, SeaTac, Tukwila and others have higher rates.

US-WI.note: 2005 Wis. Act 12 voided any local minimum wage ordinance in effect on June 16, 2005 (Madison's).

US-WV.note: West Virginia sets one statewide minimum wage in article 5C and neither authorizes nor bars a local minimum wage, and no West Virginia city or county has adopted one.

US-WY.note: Wyoming sets its statewide minimum wage in article 2 of chapter 4 and neither authorizes nor bars a local minimum wage, and no Wyoming city or county has adopted one.

us-policy-positions:labor-workforce.publ.note: Places first left out were read on 9/29/2026; any still unread take the most common answer among similar places, marked ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE.

US-AK.note: All public employees: state and local workers and teachers may bargain collectively under the Public Employment Relations Act.

US-AL.note: No bargaining statute; Alabama courts hold public agencies may not bargain absent express statutory authority, though they may meet and confer (teacher data updated January 2019).

US-AR.note: No public-sector bargaining statute; the general labor policy (Ark. Code § 11-3-301) gives no duty to bargain, so any bargaining is voluntary for the employer.

US-AS.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the most common answer among the 3 territories read for this question (2 answer yes), because this place's own law could not be read.
US-AS.note: Tried: American Samoa Code Annotated at https://asbar.org/ (HTTP 403 bot block, section search unreachable); https://www.asbar.org/ (no connection); web.archive.org (no snapshot); https://www.americansamoa.gov/ (script-rendered site with no code text); constituteproject.org (404).

US-AZ.note: No bargaining statute; public employers may only 'meet and confer' (Ariz. Att'y Gen. Op. I06-004), with some cities such as Phoenix acting by local ordinance.

US-CA.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 3502 (MMBA); §§ 3512 et seq. (Dills Act); §§ 3540 et seq. (EERA)
US-CA.note: All public employees: local government (MMBA), state (Dills Act) and school (EERA) employees have bargaining rights.

US-CO.cite: C.R.S. § 24-50-1101 et seq. (state employees, HB20-1153); C.R.S. § 8-3.3-101 et seq. (county employees, SB22-230)
US-CO.note: State employees (2020 Partnership Act) and employees of counties with 7,500+ people (from July 1, 2023); teachers and city workers bargain only where the local employer agrees.

US-CT.note: All public employees: state, municipal and teacher bargaining acts; the state code site (cga.ct.gov) was unreachable, so the fetched source shows the teacher statute only.

US-DC.note: All District government employees may bargain collectively under the Comprehensive Merit Personnel Act.

US-DE.note: State employees and local employers with 25+ full-time employees (or that opt in); teachers have a separate act (14 Del. C. ch. 40).

US-FL.cite: Fla. Const. art. I, § 6; Fla. Stat. § 447.301
US-FL.note: All public employees have a constitutional and statutory right to bargain collectively; recent laws added membership and recertification rules but kept the right.

US-GA.note: No general bargaining law; the teacher statute says nothing permits collective bargaining, and only firefighters have a local-option law (O.C.G.A. § 25-5-1 et seq.).

US-GU.note: Guam public employees may organize, and a qualified employee organization with majority support in an appropriate unit gets exclusive recognition by government management.

US-HI.note: All public employees: state and county employees and teachers bargain under HRS chapter 89, enforced by the Hawaii Labor Relations Board.

US-IA.note: All public employees keep the right, but since 2017 units with fewer than 30% public-safety members bargain only over base wages.

US-ID.note: Teachers (and firefighters under Idaho Code § 44-1801 et seq.) only; state and other local employees have no bargaining right.

US-IL.cite: 5 ILCS 315 (Illinois Public Labor Relations Act); 115 ILCS 5 (educational employees); Ill. Const. art. I, § 25
US-IL.note: All public employees: state and local workers under the Public Labor Relations Act and school employees under the Educational Labor Relations Act; a 2022 constitutional amendment added a right to bargain.

US-IN.note: Teachers only, limited to wages and benefits; state employees have had no bargaining since a 2005 executive order was rescinded, and other local employees have no statute.

US-KS.note: State employees and teachers are covered; other local employers come under the act only if their governing body elects it (the act says 'meet and confer').

US-KY.note: No general public-sector bargaining law; a public agency may choose to negotiate but has no duty to (Fayette County Educ. Ass'n v. Hardy, 1980); only some police and firefighter statutes exist.

US-LA.note: No public-sector bargaining statute; school boards and localities may bargain at their discretion (Louisiana Teachers' Ass'n v. Orleans Parish School Bd., 1974).

US-MA.note: All public employees: state, municipal and school employees bargain under chapter 150E.

US-MD.cite: Md. Code, State Pers. & Pens. § 3-501; Md. Code, Educ. §§ 6-402, 6-408
US-MD.note: State employees and public school employees bargain by statute; county and city employees depend on local law.

US-ME.note: All public employees: municipal, school, state and university employees bargain under separate acts.

US-MI.note: Local and school employees under PERA; classified state employees bargain under the Civil Service Commission's constitutional authority; the 2023 right-to-work repeal did not change this.

US-MN.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees bargain under the Public Employment Labor Relations Act.

US-MO.note: All public employees, including teachers and police, under the constitutional right to bargain as applied to the public sector in Independence-NEA v. Independence School District (2007); a 2018 restrictive law (HB 1413) was later struck down.

US-MP.note: Public employees may not strike and the Act only sets up mediation, fact-finding and arbitration of disputes, with no statutory right to organize or bargain, and wage disputes go to the Civil Service Commission.

US-MS.note: No public-sector bargaining statute; teachers may join unions but employers have no duty to bargain (Jackson v. Hazlehurst Mun. Separate School Dist., 1983).

US-MT.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees.

US-NC.note: State law declares any public-sector collective bargaining contract illegal and void.

US-ND.note: Teachers only; state and other local employees have no bargaining right.

US-NE.note: All public employees, with disputes resolved by the Commission of Industrial Relations; state employees also under the State Employees Collective Bargaining Act.

US-NH.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees bargain under RSA 273-A.

US-NJ.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees.

US-NM.note: All public employees: state and local employees and teachers; the current act (2003) reinstated bargaining after the first act expired in 1999.

US-NV.note: Local government employees and teachers since 1969; state executive-branch employees were added by SB 135 (2019).

US-NY.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees under the Taylor Law.

US-OH.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees (the 2011 SB 5 limits were repealed by referendum).

US-OK.cite: 70 O.S. § 509.6 (teachers); 11 O.S. § 51-101 et seq. (police and fire)
US-OK.note: Teachers and police/fire only; state employees have no right, and the 2004 law for general employees of large cities was repealed in 2011.

US-OR.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees.

US-PA.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees under the Public Employe Relations Act; police and fire under Act 111.

US-PR.cite: P.R. Laws, Ley 45-1998 (Ley de Relaciones del Trabajo para el Servicio Público); Ley 9-2021
US-PR.note: Central-government employees may bargain collectively under Ley 45-1998, and Ley 9-2021 (June 30, 2021) was enacted to guarantee collective bargaining.

US-RI.note: All public employees: state, municipal and school employees.

US-SC.note: Public employees have no right to collective bargaining (Branch v. City of Myrtle Beach, S.C. 2000), and no statute grants one.

US-SD.note: All public employees, including state employees, may designate representatives to meet and negotiate in good faith.

US-TN.note: No public-sector bargaining law; since 2011 teachers have only 'collaborative conferencing' on listed topics, which replaced bargaining.

US-TX.note: State law bars public employers from recognizing a union or signing a bargaining contract; only police and firefighters may bargain where local voters adopt it (Local Gov't Code ch. 143, 174).

US-UT.note: No statute gives public employees a bargaining right; HB 267 (2025) would ban it outright but was blocked on May 6, 2025 pending a November 3, 2026 referendum, and a reported December 2025 repeal was not verified here.

US-VA.note: No right: bargaining is barred unless a county, city, town or school board opts in by ordinance (allowed since May 1, 2021), and state employees are excluded.

US-VI.note: Tried: V.I. Code (Lexis-only): https://www.lexisnexis.com/hottopics/vicode/ (viewer loads, no fetchable section text); https://www.legvi.org/vicode/ (HTTP 522); https://vi.public.law/ (no connection); law.justia.com (blocked); Legislature bill-tracker PDFs (File Not Found).

US-VT.note: All public employees: state, municipal and school employees.

US-WA.note: All public employees: state, local and school employees.

US-WI.note: General municipal and school employees (and state employees) keep a right to bargain limited to total base wages since Act 10; a Dane County ruling of 12/2/2024 struck much of Act 10 but was on appeal, and either way a bargaining right existed on 1/1/2026.

US-WV.note: No public-sector bargaining statute; employers may negotiate voluntarily but no binding bargaining right exists.

US-WY.note: Only firefighters have a bargaining statute (Wyo. Stat. § 27-10-101 et seq.); school boards may bargain voluntarily (1978 Att'y Gen. opinion).
